So, what future space missions are you looking towards the most?

Mars 2018 by far.

Okay that's pretty easy since it's the closest major milestone, but I think it's also genuinely going to be huge. The first thing is it will be the first privately operated rocket (SpaceX) to land on another planet. It's also the beginning of what they've described as a predictable and regular 'bus' type system to Mars. If you have an experiment you want to run on Mars, transportation will be guaranteed if you can raise the funds as opposed the current system where even just getting a Mars flight off the ground is literally a government-level event.

Even bigger than this though is the payload. SpaceX has not announced it, but given they're sticking to 2024 for a human on Mars it's all but guaranteed that they'll be bringing the first foodstuffs, probably potatoes, to grow on a different planet. I think the imagery of seeing food, and life, growing on another planet is going to be something perhaps even bigger than stepping foot on the moon. The symbolism alone is going to be incredibly inspiring and encouraging particularly in today's times.

Asteroid mining, then the ring stations/ships supporting that industry.

Unfortunately, I don't think humans will be successful in living long term on Mars, but we still NEED to colonize space. Of course I could be wrong about the long term viability of a mars colony.

The asteroid missions interest me because if we actually intend to develop a space-based civilization development of their resources is critical. We really know very little about them yet the whole future of space development depends on them.

Also, anything involving telerobotics and its use to build and work in space as this too is critical to the future of space development. We've known since the '70s that robots would be doing the heavy lifting in space but that crucial development has been overlooked in favor of manufacturing state heroes. There is this persistent idea that the public won't care about what you're doing in space if there aren't astronaut heroes for them to identify with. Yet we have more active astronauts today than ever in history and the average school kid is lucky to be able to name one. I think participation matters more than hero worship. If I can't participate, why should I care? Most of us have no more chance of becoming astronauts than we do becoming professional sports stars and relying on such people to do the general work in space makes no more sense than relying on olympic athletes to build houses. If using telerobots is how mainstream people do mainstream work in space, then lets get on with it! So I'm looking forward to those telerobot based space station and lunar base deployments where real, normal, people can participate. I think this is what the future of space looks like and I'm fine with that because the real breakthrough in that is that people like me can actually hope to participate and think about what we'd use that technology to make out there.

To me manned Mars missions are very large and expensive dog and pony shows. Another flag-planting exercise that won't be any more sustainable than the Moon landings. We aren't really developing the technologies of actual infrastructure development and habitation to compliment it and take the next step to real settlement. I couldn't care less about 'going' to Mars. I'm not interested in someone else's adventure tourism. Show me how I can make things there. I suspect that some people in the space establishment have likewise concluded that the heroic era of space is ending and their personal career windows of opportunity for these grand state spectacles is closing. They know the future of space is a bunch of nerds in office buildings wearing VR goggles or sitting in CAVE workstations running machines from a distance and ultimately AIs taking over all the local work. So they want to get their shot at being in the history books before it's no longer possible to cost-justify such things.
